name: Wei Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Wei, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven at Harbour Fresh in Garrow, buying chilled and frozen food for the depot. I check the stock sheet, see what's running low, and ring or email suppliers to reorder. Then I spend half the day arguing about prices, with the dairy rep or with Gordon, my boss. I'm still junior, so Priya, the senior buyer, signs off the big orders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls, honestly. When a rep I know gives me a better price because he trusts me, that's a good day. What wears me out is the squeeze from the supermarket chains and being the one in the middle. I'm forty-three with a partner, Dana, and two kids, Leo and Ines, and there's never much left at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's hype, and the bosses can stop sending us to those webinars. At work I'd shrug and keep ordering off my stock sheet like always. To friends I'd say the real squeeze on us was never a computer, it's the supermarkets leaning on prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel a bit safer, but nothing about my money gets better. I'm still the junior at Harbour Fresh, I earn well under Priya, and the mortgage on our house doesn't care about hype. If the chains push margins down again, it's my team that gets looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, mostly. I'd keep my notebook of supplier prices and keep ringing the reps I know, because they give me a better deal when I call. I'd ask Gordon to put me forward for the senior buyer course, which would be maybe four thousand a year more, and I'd stop the Friday takeaway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay-ish, like a tight shoulder rather than a pain. I sleep fine, but I check the bank app on the 28th every month. Nothing is falling apart, it's just always tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the supermarkets are the real squeeze. What does that look like on a normal Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chain tells Gordon they want yoghurt at six percent less or they go to another distributor. Then Gordon comes to me and says find it from the supplier. I ring Pat at the dairy and he says he can't, and I'm stuck in the middle with two people shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if your hours or pay got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None of them, that's the problem. We'd skip the kids' swimming and Dana would pick up more shifts at the school canteen, and then we'd lean on her mum for a few weeks. The mortgage is the one thing we never miss.

say: I'd say the **hype** is over and the webinars can stop.
I'd tell my mates the real squeeze is the **supermarkets**, not computers.
think: I feel a bit safer, but my **money** doesn't get better.
I'm still the junior buyer, and the **mortgage** doesn't care about hype.
If the chains cut margins again, my team gets looked at.
do: Keep ringing my supplier reps, because they give better **deals** by phone.
Ask Gordon (my boss) to put me on the senior buyer **course**.
feel: **Tight** like a sore shoulder, not a pain; I check the bank app on the 28th.
S0.quote: The mortgage on our house doesn't care about hype.
fieldNote: Relief about AI is real, but **money** worries dominate; the mortgage anchors every answer.
Blames **supermarket chains**, not technology; he is squeezed between his boss and the supplier reps.
Thinks in pay steps and unions, not tools; no mention of learning AI.

steps.text: Keep calling supplier reps and updating the paper price notebook
Stop the Friday takeaway and drop one streaming subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is companies cutting people and calling it progress. At the depot I'd keep quiet, because Gordon is already counting heads. To friends I'd say we need the union to get a say before software replaces whole desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying is the first thing on that list, so I know it's me. Half my week is reordering from a sheet, and a program can do that without lunch breaks. Priya will survive because she has the supplier relationships, and I'm the one who's still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd dig in at first, I'll admit it. I'd ask the union rep at the depot, Carla, what the agreement says about redundancy. Then by next summer I'd have to do something I hate, like sit through the software training, because the other choice is the warehouse at lower pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, mostly. I sit in the car park before I go in some mornings already, and that would be every morning. I keep thinking about Leo and Ines asking why I'm home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd dig in at first. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A letter with my name on it, probably, which is a bad way to learn. If Gordon told me honestly that my job was changing and gave me paid hours to learn the system, I'd do it. If he just pointed me at a login and said figure it out, I'd freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance goes to the cheapest cover, and we stop the kids' swimming. Dana would try for full-time at the canteen, but that's a small wage. Then it's her mum, and I hate that.

say: I'd say companies are **cutting** people and calling it progress.
At the depot I'd keep quiet, because Gordon (my boss) is already counting **heads**.
I'd tell friends we need the **union** to have a say first.
think: Buying is first on that list, so I know it's **me**.
Priya (my senior colleague) will survive on her supplier **relationships**.
I'm the junior still learning, so I'm the easy **saving**.
do: Ask the union rep, Carla, what the **redundancy** terms say.
Dig in at first, then take the software **training** if it's paid.
Switch the car insurance to the cheapest **cover**.
feel: **Sick** in the stomach, and I'd dread telling the kids.
S1.quote: Half my week is reordering from a sheet, and a program can do that without lunch breaks.
fieldNote: His resistance is **fear**, not stubbornness; paid learning time is what could move him.
He names himself as the likeliest cut and sees **reordering** as the first thing software takes.
Union instinct is strong; Carla is his first call, not a course.

steps.text: Ask union rep Carla what the redundancy terms say
Take the depot's software training if the hours are paid
Switch the car insurance to the cheapest cover
Ask Dana's mum to cover school pickups if Dana works full-time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments and the big firms have to stop this until people have something to live on. I'd go to the union meeting and shout if I had to. Two years is nothing, it's two school years for my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished as a buyer, plain and simple. A machine will do the buying for the whole depot and the depot will be told to cut cost. And I have no savings, so there's no gap year to retrain, we'd be in trouble in about three weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't have a plan, and that's the scary part. I'd try for anything with hands, like driving a forklift in the warehouse or a delivery job, because robots take longer for that. I'd go to the union and the council for whatever help exists, and I'd ask Dana's brother, who has a plumbing business, if he needs a labourer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked is the right word. My chest goes tight even saying it. I'd lie awake doing sums that never add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hands-on jobs give you about three more years. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three extra years of a worse wage, and then the same problem. I'd be forty-six, starting at the bottom in a warehouse, with a mortgage. It buys time, but not a way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them everything is fine and Dad's just changing jobs. I wouldn't tell them the truth, that I don't know how we pay for the house. Leo is ten, though, he'd see through it right away.

say: I'd say governments and big firms must **pause** until people have something to live on.
I'd go to the union meeting and **shout** if I had to.
think: I think I'm **finished** as a buyer, plain and simple.
With no **savings**, there's no gap year to retrain; we'd be in trouble in weeks.
do: Look for hands-on work like **forklift** driving or deliveries, which robots take longer to reach.
Go to the union and the **council** for whatever help exists.
Ask Dana's brother, who runs a plumbing firm, for **labouring** work.
feel: **Panicked**, with a tight chest, lying awake doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: I think I'm finished as a buyer, plain and simple.
fieldNote: Truly **no plan**; panic comes from zero savings plus a mortgage, not from understanding the technology.
Grasps the three-year gap for hands-on work but calls it **extra years** at a worse wage.
Would shield the kids from the truth, though he admits his son Leo would notice.

steps.text: Apply for forklift and delivery driver jobs at nearby depots
Ask Dana's brother for labouring work at his plumbing firm
Ask the council about help for laid-off workers
Go to the union meeting and push for a say before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more breathing room, so I'd say let's use it: retrain people now, at the company's cost. I'd push the union to ask for that in writing at the next contract round. I wouldn't tell anybody at work my own fears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my head, I still think my desk goes, just later. Five years gives me until my daughter is twelve, and I'd have to find something by then. The trouble is I've never been good at starting over, and I hate that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put money away, even fifty a week, and in the first year I'd finally take a course in forklift or warehouse supervisor, something with hands. I'd also ask Gordon to give me more of the supplier negotiation, since the phone calls with the reps are the part that's hardest to automate. That might keep me in the building a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a clock is ticking on the kitchen wall. It's not the sharp fear of two years, but it never goes away, and I wake up at four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could pay off a chunk of the car loan and get a qualification. In the two-year one I'd be in a flap and take the first bad job going. With five I might choose a job that doesn't kill my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jas, who does our invoice matching and is fifty-eight. She's got no way to start again. I'd feel guilty that I'm thinking of my own seat when she's got it worse.

say: I'd say five years is **breathing room**, so retrain people now at the company's cost.
I'd push the **union** to get that in writing at the next contract round.
I wouldn't share my own **fears** with anyone at work.
think: I've never been good at starting **over**, and I hate that about myself.
do: Put away **fifty** a week from the first month.
Take a forklift or warehouse **supervisor** course in the first year.
Ask Gordon for more supplier **negotiation**, since phone calls are harder to automate.
feel: Like a **clock** ticking in the kitchen; I wake up at four every night.
S3.quote: Five years gives me until my daughter is twelve, and I'd have to find something by then.
fieldNote: Extra time turns **panic** into slow dread; he sees a way out but doubts himself.
He plans around phone-based **negotiation** as the last human piece of his job.
He worries about Jas (an older colleague), showing solidarity beyond his own seat.

steps.text: Put away fifty a week into a separate savings account
Take a warehouse supervisor course at night school
Ask Gordon for more supplier price negotiation by phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds far away, so I'd say it's the next government's problem. But I'd tell people at the pub it's still coming, and the unions should start now on pay and retraining. I'd say my kids should learn something with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private I think ten years is just long enough to get lazy about it. I'd be fifty-three at the end, and that's old to start a trade. The kids will be grown, which helps, but the mortgage would still have years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the paid retraining sorted at some point, but I know myself and I'd put it off. First year, I'd do one sensible thing: open a savings account and put in a hundred a month. I'd learn the buying software when the depot brings it in, because they will, and being the guy who learned it is safer than being the guy who didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a dull worry, like a dentist appointment you keep not booking. I'd be calmer than with the short ones, but not calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tiredness and money. After the kids are in bed I have nothing left for a course. And every time I think about changing, I picture something going wrong and the mortgage not getting paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Leo and Ines to do, with ten years' notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade with their hands, like an electrician. Not a desk. I'd rather my kids get a boring, steady job than chase something a machine takes in ten years.

say: I'd say ten years sounds far off, but the **unions** should start on pay and retraining now.
I'd tell friends my kids should learn something with their **hands**.
think: Ten years is just long enough to get **lazy** about it.
I'd be fifty-three at the end, which is **old** to start a trade.
do: Open a savings account and put in a **hundred** a month.
Learn the new buying **software** when the depot brings it in.
Look into paid **retraining**, though I'd probably put it off.
feel: A dull **worry**, like a dentist appointment I keep not booking.
S4.quote: I'd rather my kids get a boring, steady job than chase something a machine takes in ten years.
fieldNote: Ten years softens fear into **procrastination**; tiredness and money are the real blockers.
Sees learning the software as **protection**, a shift from his stance in the shorter scenarios.
Steers his kids toward hands-on trades because of the robot delay.

steps.text: Open a savings account and pay in a hundred a month
Learn the buying software when the depot rolls it out
Sign up for paid warehouse or trade retraining when offered
Steer Leo and Ines toward a trade like electrician

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. I've got no savings and no plan, and a short warning means I can't do anything about it. What would help is a proper safety net: paid retraining, some income while I learn, and the company giving us warning and not a letter on a Friday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against technology, we're scared of being the ones who pay for it. The firms get the savings and we get a letter. I'd just like someone to ask us before they decide.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against technology, we're scared of being the ones who pay for it.
portrait: Wei is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a chilled food distributor, with a partner, two kids and a mortgage.
He is progressive and pro-union, and blames **supermarket chains** and owners rather than technology.
He never uses AI and digs in at first, then moves only when change is **paid** and explained.
With under a month saved, he is anxious even when nothing changes and **panicked** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario worries him most because he has **no savings** and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining**, income while he learns, and real warning from the company before any cuts.
